`git rebase --onto` lets you choose where commits get replanted, separately from which commits get moved. A plain `git rebase` decides both from a single argument.

## Syntax

```
git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>]
```

This takes the commits in `<branch>` that aren't in `<upstream>` (the range `upstream..branch`) and replays them on top of `<newbase>`. If you leave out `<branch>`, it uses the current branch.

A plain `git rebase main` is the same as `git rebase --onto main main`: the cut point and the destination are both `main`. With `--onto` you can set them to different places.

## Example: move a branch off another feature branch

You branched `feature-b` from `feature-a`, but `feature-b` doesn't actually depend on `feature-a`'s work:

```
main:       A---B
                 \
feature-a:        C---D
                       \
feature-b:              E---F
```

You want only `E` and `F` on top of `main`:

```
git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b
```

Result:

```
main:       A---B
                |\
feature-a:      | C---D
                 \
feature-b:        E'---F'
```

Git took the commits reachable from `feature-b` but not from `feature-a` (`E`, `F`) and replayed them onto `main`. `C` and `D` stay out of `feature-b`. Without `--onto`, `git rebase main` on `feature-b` would have carried `C` and `D` along too.

## Other common uses

- **Drop commits from the middle of a branch:** `git rebase --onto HEAD~3 HEAD~1` removes the commits `HEAD~2` and `HEAD~1` and keeps only the newest commit, replayed onto `HEAD~3`.
- **After an upstream branch was squash-merged or rewritten:** `git rebase --onto main <old-feature-a-tip> feature-b` moves only your own commits, so the stale copies of the upstream commits don't come along.

Rebasing rewrites commit hashes (`E'`, `F'`), so if the branch was already pushed you'll need `git push --force-with-lease`.
